name: Khan-Penrose Colliding Plane Waves
description: Two impulsive plane gravitational waves colliding head on in flat space. Each focuses the other, and the vacuum where both have passed ends in a spacelike curvature singularity.
convention: No coordinate carries dimensions of time, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
history: Maxwell's equations are linear, so two electromagnetic waves pass straight through each other, and no such principle of superposition holds for gravitational waves travelling in different directions [szekeres1970]. K. A. Khan and Roger Penrose found in 1971 the exact vacuum spacetime in which two plane gravitational waves, each an impulsive wave, collide head on [khan1971]. The fronts of the two waves are the null hypersurfaces $u = 0$ and $v = 0$, and on each the Riemann tensor has a delta singularity [luk2017, frauendiener2014].¶Ahead of both waves space is flat, and behind either wave alone it is flat again, with the metric $-2L^2du\,dv + (1 + u)^2dx^2 + (1 - u)^2dy^2$ behind the wave that crosses $u = 0$ [frauendiener2014]. There the null rays running across the front converge in $y$ and meet at $u = 1$, where the flat region ends in a fold singularity with the curvature still zero [frauendiener2014]. Where both waves have passed, $u > 0$ and $v > 0$, each focuses the other, and the curvature grows without bound toward a spacelike curvature singularity along $u^2 + v^2 = 1$, formed in vacuum from the collision alone [khan1971, frauendiener2014].¶Peter Szekeres wrote in 1970 that "nowhere should the nonlinear features of general relativity show up more clearly than in the collisional interaction of two gravitational waves", and gave a solution "representing at least a portion of such a collisional situation" [szekeres1970]. Two years later he derived the equations for the collision of two plane gravitational waves and found their general exact solution when both waves are linearly polarized [szekeres1972]. He read the singular behaviour as "just another aspect of Penrose's result that plane gravitational waves act as a perfect astigmatic lens", and judged that waves with curved fronts "may still act as imperfect lenses providing a certain degree of focusing and amplification for each other" [szekeres1972, luk2017]. A plane wave focuses the null cones through it so strongly that no spacelike surface in the spacetime can carry Cauchy data for the whole of it, as Penrose had shown in 1965 [penrose1965plane].¶Impulsive waves whose polarizations are not aligned collide in an exact solution that Yavuz Nutku and Mustafa Halil found in 1977, writing the collision of plane waves with two polarizations as a harmonic map between Riemannian manifolds, and it reduces to Khan and Penrose's when the polarizations are aligned [nutku1977]. For spacetimes with two spacelike Killing vectors the vacuum equations reduce to a single equation of the Ernst type, and Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar and Valeria Ferrari, who carried out the reduction in 1984, found that its simplest linear solution is the Nutku-Halil solution [chandrasekhar1984ferrari]. In their words, the Nutku-Halil solution "in some sense" occupies the same place among those spacetimes "as the Kerr solution does in space-times with one time-like and one space-like Killing-vector" [chandrasekhar1984ferrari]. Chandrasekhar and Basilis Xanthopoulos found in 1986 an exact solution for colliding plane impulsive gravitational waves accompanied by shock waves [chandrasekhar1986]. Their collision produces a null surface that acts like an event horizon [chandrasekhar1986]. Beyond it the spacetime extends to timelike curvature singularities along two hyperbolic arcs, "reminiscent of the ring singularity of the Kerr metric" [chandrasekhar1986].¶Frank Tipler gave in 1980 a geometrical argument that a collision between two plane gravitational waves must result in singularities [tipler1980]. He suggested that the singular structure of the Khan-Penrose solution is an artifact of plane symmetry [tipler1980, luk2017]. With Richard Matzner he showed in 1984 that "the apparently local curvature singularities both in the Khan-Penrose solution and in the Bell-Szekeres solution are actually global" [matzner1984]. Near the singularity of a collision of plane waves with parallel polarizations the metric approaches an inhomogeneous Kasner solution, as Ulvi Yurtsever showed in 1988, with exponents along the singularity fixed by the data on the fronts of the incoming waves [yurtsever1988]. Special choices of those data turn the curvature singularity into a Killing-Cauchy horizon, which is unstable against small generic perturbations of the data, and generic data produce "all-embracing, spacelike curvature singularities without Killing-Cauchy horizons" [yurtsever1988].¶Jörg Frauendiener, Chris Stevens, and Ben Whale approached the Khan-Penrose solution numerically in 2014, approximating each impulsive profile by a sequence of smooth ones [frauendiener2014]. After the collision each wave keeps a strengthened impulsive part in its profile and picks up a tail [frauendiener2014]. Jonathan Luk and Igor Rodnianski proved in 2017 that two impulsive gravitational waves of finite extent, with fronts of any curvature and no symmetry assumed, interact with their curvature delta singularities propagating along null hypersurfaces that intersect, and that the spacetime stays smooth away from the waves after their first interaction [luk2017].

related.text: Near the singularity made by the collision the metric approaches a Kasner solution whose exponents vary along the singularity [yurtsever1988].
Each incoming wave alone is a plane wave of this family. Roger Penrose showed in 1965 how strongly such a wave focuses light [penrose1965plane].
The calm before the collision. Spacetime is flat ahead of both waves, and flat again behind either one alone [frauendiener2014].

coordinates.name: Cosmological

parameters.description: Focal length of each wave, in the frame where the two are equal: behind one wave alone the null rays across its front meet at $u = 1$ or $v = 1$.

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, \sigma, x, y)$ where both waves have passed, with $\tau = \arcsin u + \arcsin v$ and $\sigma = \arcsin u - \arcsin v$ dimensionless, and $x$ and $y$ lengths across the wave fronts.
